mappings.note: Who wrote 'The Summit Within' -- knowing the text one has read, not a detail inside it, so the read-with-comprehension LO rather than LO-71.
His most dominant feeling on the summit -- a point stated in the essay.
Completing 'the ___ in me seemed to say ...' -- recall of a stated line.
Why there was a tinge of sadness -- a reason given in the essay.
Completing 'the man who has been to the ___ is never the same again' -- recall of a stated line.
What the OTHER summit is -- requires reading the title's metaphor against the essay's argument, which is LO-72's critical reading; LO-71 would make a figure of speech a plain detail.
His personal answer to 'why do people climb mountains' -- a point stated in the essay.
What a climb to the summit means -- a stated definition in the essay.
What 'exhilarating' means in the quoted sentence -- inferring an unfamiliar word from context, the vocabulary LO.
Mountains as a means of communion with ___ -- recall of a stated line.
The answer to 'why Everest' -- a point stated in the essay.
What the author calls the change he felt -- a stated term in the essay.
Completing 'it is a challenge difficult to ___' -- recall of a stated line.
What the Everest climber becomes conscious of -- a point stated in the essay.
What the experience is -- a stated description.
What famous climbers have left records of -- stated detail.
Completing 'you ___ every nerve as you take another step' -- recall of a stated line.
Why you curse yourself -- a reason given in the essay.
What you tell yourself on the summit -- a stated line.
What the surrounding peaks look like -- a stated description.
Whose picture he left on Everest -- stated detail.
Why you bow down at the peak -- a reason given in the essay.
What each man carries within himself -- a stated line of the essay.
Why one must climb the summit within -- asks the reader to relate the essay's idea to life, which LO-72 names; LO-71 would treat an argument as a fact.
Whether the mountain summit resembles the summit within -- an explicit compare-and-contrast, which LO-72 names.
What the climb certainly does to you -- a point stated in the essay.
What being an Everester has given him -- a point stated in the essay.
How the internal summits compare with the outer ones -- a comparison the reader must draw, so LO-72.
The year he climbed Everest -- stated detail.
Whether he climbed alone -- stated detail.

Who wrote 'The School Boy' -- a poem item filed under this prose chapter, and LO-76 is the only outcome that names poems.
Completing 'I ___ to rise on a summer morn' -- a line of the poem.
What the boy likes about the huntsman -- a point in the poem.
Who sings along with the school boy -- a point in the poem.
What drives all the joy away -- the poem's central complaint.
Completing 'the little ones spend the day in ___ and ___' -- a line of the poem.
Completing 'nor in my ___ can I take delight' -- a line of the poem.
Whom he compares himself to in the quoted stanza -- reading the poem's image of the drooping bird.
Whom he addresses in 'if buds are nip'd' -- the poem's closing appeal.
Completing the poem's closing question about the summer fruits -- a line of the poem.
'Right now I ... a book on how to cook' -- present continuous, grammar rather than a poem item.
'We ... three major snowstorms so far this winter' -- present perfect, grammar.
